content: In organic chemistry, a thiol is a compound that contains a functional group consisting of a sulfur atom bonded to a hydrogen atom (-SH). This group is the sulfur analogue of the hydroxyl group (-OH) found in alcohols. The functional group is referred to as either a thiol group or a sulfhydryl group. Traditionally, thiols are also known as mercaptans. When naming thiols, several conventions are used. The preferred method, as per IUPAC guidelines, involves adding the suffix -thiol to the name of the parent alkane. For example, CH₃SH is named methanethiol. An older naming method replaces the term alcohol in the name of the corresponding alcohol compound with mercaptan. For instance, CH₃SH would be called methyl mercaptan, analogous to methyl alcohol (CH₃OH). Additionally, the prefix mercaptocan be used, as in the compound mercaptopurine. The term mercaptan originates from the Latin words mercurius captans, meaning seizing mercury, because the –SH group binds strongly to mercury. Many thiols are colorless liquids with a strong, often unpleasant odor resembling garlic. Low molecular weight thiols are particularly pungent and can bind strongly to skin proteins, causing persistent odors, such as those produced by skunk spray. Thiols are also added to odorless natural gas (e.g., ethanethiol) to provide a detectable smell for safety purposes, a practice initiated after the 1937 New London School explosion in Texas. However, not all thiols have unpleasant odors; for example, grapefruit mercaptan, a monoterpenoid thiol, is responsible for the characteristic scent of grapefruit. The boiling points and solubility of thiols are influenced by the weak polarity of the S-H bond, which is nearly nonpolar due to the small electronegativity difference between sulfur and hydrogen. As a result, thiols exhibit minimal hydrogen bonding with water or among themselves, leading to lower boiling points and reduced solubility in water compared to alcohols of similar molecular weight. Thiols have boiling points and solubility comparable to isomeric sulfides. The synthesis of thiols is analogous to the methods used for alcohols and ethers, but the reactions are faster and yield higher products because sulfur anions are better nucleophiles than oxygen atoms. Thiols can be synthesized by heating a halogenoalkane with a solution of sodium hydrosulfide. Disulfides can also be reduced by agents like lithium aluminum hydride in dry ether to form two thiols. Chemically, the thiol group is the sulfur analogue of the hydroxyl group (-OH) in alcohols. Sulfur and oxygen, being in the same periodic group, share similar bonding properties. Thiols can form thioethers, thioacetals, and thioesters, which are analogous to ethers, acetals, and esters, respectively. Thiols can also react with alkenes to form thioethers, a reaction that is biochemically significant as thiol groups can react with vinyl groups to form thioether linkages. The sulfur atom in a thiol is highly nucleophilic, more so than the oxygen atom in an alcohol. Thiols are moderately acidic, with a typical pKa of around 10 to 11. In the presence of a base, thiolates (RS⁻) are formed, which are highly reactive nucleophiles. Thiols and their corresponding anions are readily oxidized by reagents like bromine to form organic disulfides (R-S-S-R). Stronger oxidizing agents, such as sodium hypochlorite or hydrogen peroxide, can further oxidize thiols to sulfonic acids (RSO₃H). Biologically, the thiol group plays a critical role as the functional group of the amino acid cysteine. When two cysteine residues are brought into proximity during protein folding, an oxidation reaction can form a disulfide bond (-S-S-), creating a cystine unit. These disulfide bonds contribute to the tertiary structure of proteins if the cysteines are part of the same peptide chain, or to the quaternary structure of multi-unit proteins by forming strong covalent bonds between different peptide chains. For example, the heavy and light chains of antibodies are held together by disulfide bridges. Disulfide bonds are also responsible for the structural kinks in curly hair. Hair treatments like permanent waves exploit the oxidizability of cysteine residues: reducing agents break disulfide bonds to free cysteine sulfhydryl groups, while oxidizing agents reform disulfide bonds to create new hair shapes. In enzymes, sulfhydryl groups in active sites can form noncovalent bonds with substrates, contributing to catalytic activity. Active site cysteine residues are the functional units in cysteine proteases.
